newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan urges East Asian nations to shun nationalism.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan urges East Asian nations to shun nationalism.

text.p: Taiwan President Lee Teng-hui urged East Asian countries on Friday to forgo nationalism for political integration.
He made the call in a statement presented to an academic seminar in Osaka, Japan, on Friday, the 51st anniversary of Taiwan's emergence from Japanese rule.
Tokyo has no diplomatic ties with Taipei and Lee has not been allowed to visit.

The statement was presented a day after Taiwan blocked a protest by local activists who had planned to mark Friday by dropping flags on a group of disputed islands in the East China Sea to challenge Japan's claim of sovereignty.
"To solve the (security) problem, East Asian nations must gradually walk towards integration of international politics," Lee said in the statement.
"To integrate, (East Asian nations) must give up inappropriate nationalism."
The statement was faxed to Reuters by the presidential office.
Lee noted rising economic interdependence among East Asian nations. "But East Asia so far still has no integrated security system to reduce security worries by each country."
Friday was the anniversary of Taiwan's 1945 freedom from a half-century of Japanese colonial rule, but Lee did not mention Japan by name.

Japanese right-wingers sparked a nationalistic backlash from Chinese across Asia after raising Japan's flag and building a lighthouse on the disputed islands, claimed by Japan as the Senkakus and by Taiwan and China as the Diaoyus.

On October 7, Taiwan and Hong Kong activists pierced a Japanese maritime cordon and planted on one of the islands flags of Taiwan's exiled Republic of China and the communist People's Republic of China.
In his statement, Lee said economic development had promoted democracy and liberalisation in East Asia.

"Even in mainland China, economic development has triggered many internal changes. (I) believe in the beginning of the next century, (the) mainland's communist system will definitely be replaced by a free and democratic system," he said.
He also reiterated his willingness to talk with his Chinese counterparts, seeking way to ease tensions between the two sides.
In Beijing on Friday, China said Taiwan was a pawn and toy of hostile Western forces out to weaken and divide the country and thwart its development.
"Taiwan...acts as a pawn of international anti-Chinese forces, a toy in the hands of others," said a front-page commentary in the People's Daily, the ruling Communist Party's official newspaper.
China, which regards Taiwan as a rebel province since the end of a civil war in 1949, launched missile tests north of the island after Lee's landmark June 1995 U.S. visit.
China sees Taiwan's efforts to break out of its diplomatic isolation as an attempt to move towards independence from China.
Taiwan, which agrees the island is a part of China, says its diplomatic initiatives are aimed at smoothing the path towards eventual reunification with China.
